articles.title: Sara Rowbotham: the Rochdale health worker who raised 181 safeguarding alerts
articles.excerpt: Sara Rowbotham repeatedly raised concerns about vulnerable young people while working for Rochdale’s Crisis Intervention Team, later giving evidence to Parliament about the response to child sexual exploitation in the town.
articles.content_html:
Sara Rowbotham became one of the most recognisable figures associated with the response to child sexual exploitation in Rochdale after repeatedly raising concerns about vulnerable young people while working for the town’s NHS Crisis Intervention Team.

Rowbotham worked as the Crisis Intervention Team Co-ordinator and Sexual Health Improvement Specialist. The team was established in 2004 and supported thousands of young people, including those who disclosed concerns about sexual abuse and exploitation.

In evidence to the House of Commons Home Affairs Committee in November 2012, Rowbotham told MPs that, over a period covering the years from 2005 to 2011, her team had identified referrals involving 103 young people.

She also told the committee that she had made 181 alerts to Children’s Social Care about concerns involving young people.

Asked whether she believed police and social services had worked together effectively, Rowbotham said this had happened “very rarely” in the early period and that she had subsequently begun making the Safeguarding Children Unit aware of the referrals so that strategy meetings could be convened.

The committee also heard evidence from other senior officials about the handling of the information. The subsequent Home Affairs Committee report described missed opportunities and examined the response of children's social care and police to child sexual exploitation in Rochdale.

Rowbotham told MPs that she had repeatedly tried to make protective services aware of the vulnerability of young people and that she believed agencies had failed to provide a sufficiently comprehensive and coordinated response.

The evidence came after the prosecution of nine men in Rochdale in 2012 for serious sexual offences against girls. The case prompted wider scrutiny of how authorities had responded to reports of child sexual exploitation.

Rowbotham continued to speak publicly about the response. In 2014, she was made redundant from her role. Contemporary reporting by ITV News and The Guardian documented her concerns about the handling of the case and the impact of losing her position.

Her story later reached a much wider audience when the BBC drama Three Girls was broadcast in May 2017, with Maxine Peake portraying Rowbotham.

A petition calling for Rowbotham to be formally recognised attracted more than 100,000 signatures within days of the programme airing and ultimately exceeded 275,000 signatures, according to contemporary reports.

Rowbotham subsequently entered local politics. She was elected as a councillor for North Middleton in 2015 and went on to serve as Deputy Leader of Rochdale Borough Council and as a cabinet member.

Her public recognition also continued. She received a Special Recognition Award at the NHS Heroes Awards in 2018 and was made an honorary member of the NSPCC Council that year. In 2021, she was appointed MBE for services to young people.

Rowbotham’s evidence to Parliament remains part of the official record of the scrutiny that followed the Rochdale child sexual exploitation cases. Her account of the 181 alerts, and questions about how information held by frontline services was acted upon, formed part of the wider examination of safeguarding failures in the town.

Source: House of Commons Home Affairs Committee evidence and report; contemporary reporting by ITV News and The Guardian; Rochdale Borough Council records.

articles.excerpt: The Restore Britain Burnley & Hyndburn Branch has announced an evening event featuring guest speakers Charlie Downes and Montgomery Toms on Friday 16 October.
articles.content_html:
The Restore Britain Burnley & Hyndburn Branch has announced an evening event featuring guest speakers Charlie Downes and Montgomery Toms on Friday 16 October 2026.

According to the organisers, the event will take place from 7pm until 1am, with doors opening at 6.30pm.

The organisers say the evening will include speeches from Charlie Downes and Montgomery Toms, a light buffet and entertainment, alongside an opportunity for attendees to meet other members from across the North West.

Tickets are being sold by the organisers, with numbers described as limited.

The event is being promoted by the Restore Britain Burnley & Hyndburn Branch. Rochdale Daily has not independently verified the organisers’ ticket availability or other event arrangements.

articles.title: New Awaab’s Law protections could cover millions more renters and vulnerable households
articles.excerpt: A government consultation will examine extending Awaab’s Law to private renters and other accommodation, with faster legal deadlines for landlords to tackle serious hazards such as damp and mould.
articles.content_html:
Millions more households could receive stronger legal protections against dangerous housing conditions under plans to extend Awaab’s Law beyond social housing.

The Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government has launched a consultation on how the law could be introduced for private renters and whether similar protections should apply to other forms of accommodation.

Awaab’s Law currently provides legal deadlines for social landlords to investigate and address serious hazards, including dangerous damp and mould. The measures were introduced in memory of two-year-old Awaab Ishak, who died in 2020 after prolonged exposure to damp and mould in his home.

The proposed extension could mean around nine million households are covered by new repair timescales, compared with around four million currently covered.

The consultation is considering protections for private rented homes as well as:

temporary accommodation for homeless people and families;

accommodation for young people leaving care; and

supported housing, including accommodation used by older, disabled and other vulnerable people.

Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook said all renters should be able to expect a safe and decent home, regardless of tenure.

“Awaab’s Law is already helping to drive up standards in the social housing sector. We’re now moving to extend it to private landlords so that England’s 11 million private renters can enjoy the same protections,” he said.

The government says landlords are already required to act when serious hazards are identified. Around one in 10 private rented homes is estimated to contain a Category 1 hazard, the most serious level.

The Renters’ Rights Act has also introduced fines of up to £7,000 where serious dangers are found. Awaab’s Law would add legally defined timescales requiring action on the most serious conditions.

The consultation will help determine how Awaab’s Law should operate in the private rented sector, including the timescales for the new protections to come into force. It closes on 18 December 2026.

Generation Rent welcomed the move. Chief Executive Holly Williamson said too many renters live in homes that can harm their health and wait months for landlords to address problems.

Crisis also backed the proposals, highlighting the conditions faced by people living in temporary accommodation, including hostels and bed and breakfasts.

The Renters’ Reform Coalition said nobody should have to live in a home that makes them ill or puts their life at risk, while Independent Age said older renters can face serious problems including rats and mould and may be afraid to request repairs.

Independent Age said almost 96% of older renters it polled supported Awaab’s Law.

Become, the national charity for children in care and young care leavers, also welcomed the government’s consideration of stronger standards for accommodation used by young people leaving care.

The proposals form part of commitments in the Renters’ Rights Act and the National Plan to End Homelessness.

The government says the changes are intended to ensure dangerous housing conditions are dealt with quickly and that tenants can raise concerns without fear of repercussions.

Source: Ministry of Housing, Communities & Local Government.

articles.title: Construction Begins on New 103,770 sq ft Industrial Unit at Birch Business Park, Heywood
articles.excerpt: A new urban logistics unit, Birch 100, is under construction at Birch Business Park in Heywood, expected to enhance local industrial operations and create jobs by summer 2027.
articles.content_html:
Construction has commenced on a new 103,770 square foot urban logistics unit at Birch Business Park in Heywood. The facility, named Birch 100, is being developed in the south-east corner of the 15.6-hectare estate, which is strategically located near junction 3 of the M66 and junction 19 of the M62.

The site was previously used for the storage of portacabins, cranes, and other construction equipment. The new unit will be occupied by McCarthy and Stone, which plans to use the facility for the maintenance of heavy goods vehicles (HGVs) and cranes, as well as a fuelling point.

Chancerygate, the urban logistics developer and investment manager, is overseeing the project and will also refurbish three additional units within the estate. The completion of Birch 100 is anticipated for summer 2027, contributing to the ongoing expansion of the Northern Gateway, a 1,600-acre employment area straddling the borders of Bury and Rochdale.

The Northern Gateway project aims to establish one of the largest employment hubs in the region, with plans for 6.5 million square feet of industrial space and the potential to create up to 10,000 jobs in Greater Manchester. Mike Walker, head of Chancerygate’s North West office, highlighted the importance of this development in meeting the demand for quality, sustainable industrial space in the area.

articles.title: Rochdale Engineer Develops AI Prototype for Captioning Phone Conversations
articles.excerpt: A deaf engineer from Rochdale has created an AI prototype designed to caption phone conversations, enhancing communication accessibility for the hearing impaired.
articles.content_html:
A deaf engineer from Rochdale has developed an AI prototype aimed at captioning phone conversations. This technology seeks to improve communication for individuals who are hard of hearing, making phone calls more accessible.

The prototype employs advanced speech recognition algorithms to transcribe spoken words into text in real-time, allowing users to read the conversation as it unfolds.

The engineer's work addresses a critical gap in communication tools available for the deaf and hard of hearing community. The project has gained attention for its potential to transform how individuals engage in phone conversations.

Next steps for the prototype include further testing and potential collaboration with organisations focused on accessibility to refine the technology and explore its practical applications.

articles.title: Rail Regulator Rejects Plans for Rochdale to London Euston Train Services
articles.excerpt: The Office of Rail and Road has rejected proposals for new train services between Rochdale and London Euston, citing concerns over capacity on the West Coast Main Line.
articles.content_html:
Plans to introduce up to four daily train services between Rochdale and London Euston have been rejected by the Office of Rail and Road (ORR). The regulator stated that adding more trains to the already congested West Coast Main Line would likely lead to increased delays and cancellations for passengers.

The proposal, put forward by low-cost rail operator Lumo, aimed to establish services running on weekdays and Saturdays, with three return services on Sundays. The plans had received support from Rochdale MP Paul Waugh, who advocated for improved rail connectivity for the area.

In its announcement, the ORR explained that the capacity and performance of the southern section of the West Coast Main Line had not materially changed since similar applications were rejected in 2025. An external review commissioned by the ORR supported this conclusion, indicating that the current timetable needs to allow for recovery during disruptions to minimise delays.

Stephanie Tobyn, ORR's director of strategy, policy and reform, emphasised the importance of maintaining resilience on the rail network. She noted that while new services can benefit passengers, the existing pressure on the West Coast Main Line must be addressed to avoid worsening reliability for all users. The ORR also rejected applications from other operators seeking to add services on the same line, reinforcing the challenges faced by the current rail infrastructure.

articles.title: Mossylea Housing Development in Middleton Shortlisted for Two National Awards
articles.excerpt: First Choice Homes Oldham's £7.1 million Mossylea development in Middleton has been recognised as a finalist in two categories at the Inside Housing Awards, highlighting its commitment to affordable housing.
articles.content_html:
First Choice Homes Oldham’s £7.1 million Mossylea housing development in Middleton has been shortlisted for two categories at the Inside Housing Awards. The 29-home scheme is a finalist for both best affordable suburban housing development and best suburban shared ownership development.

Mossylea is one of nine finalists in each category, with the affordable housing development category attracting over 300 entries, a record for the awards. Built on the site of a former school, the development includes two two-bedroom bungalows, three two-bedroom houses, and 24 three-bedroom houses. Of the total, 21 properties are designated for affordable rent, while eight are available for shared ownership.

All homes at Mossylea have achieved an Energy Performance Certificate rating of A, featuring solar panels, enhanced insulation, efficient heating systems, and electric vehicle charging points. Andy Ewart, FCHO’s executive director of corporate services and deputy chief executive, praised the contributions of the developer Lancet Homes and the project’s architects MPSL Planning & Design, stating they did a tremendous job on the project.

The Inside Housing Awards aim to celebrate excellence in the housing sector, and the recognition for Mossylea underscores the importance of affordable housing solutions in the region. The winners will be announced at a ceremony later this year, with the awards serving to highlight innovative approaches to housing development across the UK.

articles.title: High Court Rules Against Hopwood DePree in Ownership Dispute Over Hopwood Hall
articles.excerpt: The High Court in Manchester has ruled that Rochdale Council acted fairly in denying ownership of Hopwood Hall to Hopwood DePree, a descendant of the original owners.
articles.content_html:
A High Court ruling has determined that Rochdale Council did not act unfairly in its decision to deny ownership of Hopwood Hall to Hopwood DePree, a descendant of the family that originally built the historic property in the 1420s. The ruling concluded a two-day trial held in Manchester, where DePree had sought to overturn the council's decision to terminate an exclusivity agreement for the sale of the Grade II-listed hall.

Following the verdict, DePree expressed disappointment, stating it was a significant setback for both the community and heritage rescue groups across the UK. He indicated that his legal team is currently exploring potential next steps in response to the ruling. DePree emphasised the importance of monitoring the council's efforts to preserve and restore Hopwood Hall for public benefit.

Hopwood Hall has a rich history, having been owned by the Hopwood family until 1922, after which it changed hands multiple times. The building was used as a Catholic teacher training college until the 1980s, after which it fell into disrepair. Rochdale Council acquired the property to prevent further deterioration and has since been involved in discussions regarding its future.

The ruling may have implications for the future of Hopwood Hall, as the council continues to seek ways to restore the building and engage the community in its preservation. The next steps for both the council and DePree remain to be seen as they navigate the aftermath of this legal decision.

articles.title: Why Rochdale says ‘cruckle’
articles.excerpt: Cruckle — the local verb for rolling or twisting an ankle — is a small word with deep dialect roots and a big place in Rochdale identity.
articles.summary: Cruckle — the local verb for rolling or twisting an ankle — is a small word with deep dialect roots and a big place in Rochdale identity.
articles.body:
If you grew up in Rochdale you have probably heard someone say, “I cruckled my ankle.” Around here, to cruckle means to roll or twist the ankle in that awkward, half‑stumble you can sometimes walk off — the kind of misstep that makes you hop for a second and mutter under your breath.

That everyday meaning matches how local people use the word today, but cruckle is not an accidental invention of modern youths. Linguistic evidence shows it belongs to an older family of northern dialect verbs with senses around bending, huddling, stooping and moving crookedly. Comparative dialect material recorded forms such as cruggle, krukel, crookle and similar spellings in Scots and northern English sources; the sense of “making crooked or crouching” naturally extends to hobbling or going over on a foot, which explains the Rochdale sense.

Two kinds of evidence help explain why Rochdale claims cruckle. First, historical dialect lexicons preserve cognates: entries in regional and Scots dictionaries record cruggle/cruckle/krukel variants with meanings like “to crouch” or “to huddle.” Those entries show the word family is old and distributed across northern varieties of English and Scots, not a modern one‑street coinage.

Second, recent perceptual‑dialect research (Greater Manchester, 2024) shows that speakers across the city‑region explicitly associate the word with Rochdale. In that study — which used folk labels, draw‑a‑map and keyword prompts — many respondents named cruckle among the terms they felt characterised Rochdale speech. In other words, even if related forms exist elsewhere historically, contemporary social perception pins the word to Rochdale: people in and around the borough identify it as one of their local markers.

How did the meaning narrow to “roll an ankle”? The morphological pattern helps explain this shift. The crook/krug root (ideas of bending or crookedness) combined with a frequentative or diminutive ‑le ending yields verbs describing small repeated or awkward movements. From “bend/stoop/hobble” it is a short semantic step to an action that produces a crooked gait or sudden bend of the foot — i.e. rolling an ankle. That pathway is consistent with how many dialect verbs change sense over time.

What does this tell us about dialect and place? Small words such as cruckle are useful windows into both history and identity. Linguistically, they show continuity with older regional word families recorded in nineteenth‑ and twentieth‑century sources. Socially, they act as identity tokens: being able to use (or recognise) cruckle marks someone as local or connected to Rochdale. The recent perceptual work makes this explicit by measuring which words people put on the map when asked where certain speech belongs.

Two important cautions. First, cruckle’s reputation as a strictly “Rochdale‑only” word is mostly a matter of modern perception and local pride: historical forms appear in wider northern dialect material, so it is not entirely unprecedented elsewhere. Second, while the 2024 study captures how people label and recognise the word, it is not a full frequency survey of everyday speech; we cannot precisely quantify how often people use cruckle on the streets today without a dedicated corpus study.

For readers, cruckle is a neat local survival: an old northern verb-family preserved in a form and meaning that has come to signal Rochdale speech. It’s one of those tiny words that tie ordinary daily life — the occasional twisted ankle — to a longer story about language, movement and belonging in our borough.

articles.title: Rochdale Council Proposes Investment in Education and Inclusion Services
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has put forward a proposal to invest in central schools services funding aimed at enhancing statutory education and inclusion across the borough.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has proposed an investment of Central Schools Services Block funding to support statutory education and inclusion. This initiative aims to enhance educational services and ensure that all students receive necessary support in their learning environments.

The proposal was detailed in a report presented to the Schools Forum, highlighting the importance of adequate funding for educational services that cater to diverse needs within the community.

Next steps will involve discussions with stakeholders to refine the proposal and determine the allocation of funds. The council is committed to ensuring that the investment translates into tangible improvements in educational services for Rochdale's children.

articles.title: Rochdale AFC to Support Play Safe Campaign This Weekend
articles.excerpt: Rochdale AFC will participate in the Play Safe campaign this weekend, promoting safety in youth football. The initiative aims to raise awareness about safeguarding in the sport.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale AFC has announced its support for the Play Safe campaign this weekend, which focuses on promoting safety and safeguarding in youth football. The initiative encourages clubs, coaches, and parents to prioritise the welfare of young players.

The Play Safe campaign aims to ensure that children involved in football are protected and that their experiences are positive and safe. This campaign is particularly relevant as it coincides with the start of the football season, when many young players are returning to the pitch.

As part of the campaign, Rochdale AFC will engage with its community to raise awareness about safeguarding practices. The club is expected to share resources and information with parents and coaches throughout the weekend.

Local supporters are encouraged to participate in the campaign by attending matches and engaging with the club's activities.

articles.title: Former Rochdale Takeaway Penalised for Deliberate Tax Default
articles.excerpt: PJ Rochdale Ltd, previously a Papa John's franchise, has been fined over £149,000 for failing to pay taxes. The penalty follows HMRC's investigation into deliberate tax defaults.
articles.content_html:
PJ Rochdale Ltd, which formerly operated as a franchise of Papa John's at 3 Mellor Street, Rochdale, has been penalised for a deliberate tax default amounting to £149,650.16. The penalty was issued after the company failed to pay £213,785.95 in taxes earned between July 5, 2018, and August 31, 2023.

The details of the penalty were published in HMRC's updated list of deliberate tax defaulters, which includes businesses and individuals who have incurred penalties for providing inaccurate documents or failing to comply with tax obligations. This list is part of HMRC's civil proceedings and does not include criminal convictions.

PJ Rochdale Ltd is among 11 businesses and individuals in Greater Manchester named in this latest disclosure, which highlights over 130 cases nationally. HMRC stated that these deliberate acts resulted in the establishment of an additional tax amount exceeding £50,000.

The publication of this information serves as a warning to other businesses regarding the importance of compliance with tax regulations. It is unclear what immediate actions the company will take following this penalty, but it may impact their operations and reputation in the local community.

articles.title: 590 Bus Service from Rochdale to Halifax Showcases Scenic Pennine Journey
articles.excerpt: The 590 bus service from Rochdale to Halifax offers passengers a picturesque view of Greater Manchester's industrial heritage and beautiful landscapes for just £2.50.
articles.content_html:
The 590 bus service from Rochdale to Halifax has been praised for its scenic journey across the Pennines, providing passengers with a view of the region's rich industrial heritage and picturesque landscapes. Operated by First Bus, the service departs from Rochdale bus station and travels through Smallbridge and Littleborough before crossing into West Yorkshire.

The journey begins in Rochdale's urban area, which soon gives way to the scenic Calder Valley. Notable sights along the route include the gritstone ridge of Blackstone Edge and the historic Summit Tunnel, designed by George Stephenson. This tunnel, which opened in 1841, was once the longest railway tunnel in the world and is a significant piece of Victorian engineering. It was also the site of a major underground fire in 1984, highlighting its historical importance.

Passengers can also enjoy views of the Rochdale Canal, one of the highest canals in England, historically used for transporting goods between Lancashire and Yorkshire. Today, the canal is frequented by pleasure cruisers and kayakers, enhancing the charm of the journey. The bus route offers glimpses of local wildlife, including a herd of alpacas grazing near the canal, adding to the scenic experience.

The 590 service operates at a single ticket price of £2.50, reflecting its private ownership. This affordable option allows residents and visitors to explore the natural beauty and historical significance of the area, connecting two towns while highlighting the region's industrial past. The bus route not only serves as a means of transport but also as a journey through the rich tapestry of the Pennines' heritage.

articles.title: From historic chapel to bridal sanctuary: Orla Bridal celebrates its launch in Mytholmroyd
articles.excerpt: A new independent bridal boutique has opened in one of Mytholmroyd’s historic buildings, bringing a new chapter of celebration to The Chapel on Scout Road.
articles.content_html:
A new independent bridal boutique has opened in one of Mytholmroyd’s historic buildings, bringing a fresh chapter of celebration to The Chapel on Scout Road.

Founded by Littleborough businesswomen Jessica Demain and Delphine Gott, Orla Bridal marked its launch on Saturday 3 October with a celebration attended by family, friends and local businesses who helped bring their vision to life.

The pair have created a warm, welcoming bridal sanctuary, combining the building’s character with sparkling chandeliers, thoughtful interiors and a collection of designer gowns from Justin Alexander, Madi Lane and Modeca. Visits are private and by appointment only, giving each bride the space and personal attention to enjoy finding her dress with her closest guests.

Originally built in 1806, the Methodist chapel was extended to accommodate a Sunday school in 1872. Acquired by The Craggs Country Business Parks in 2018, it was sensitively restored and transformed into offices, preserving its heritage for a new generation.

Now, Orla is bringing something of the building’s original spirit back to its rooms: a place to gather, share meaningful moments and celebrate love.

For Jess and Delphine, that sense of occasion and belonging is at the heart of the business. Their vision is for every bride to feel comfortable, celebrated and free to be herself, surrounded by beautiful dresses in a calm and supportive setting.

Saturday’s launch offered guests a first look at the boutique, with flowers, fizz and cakes marking the culmination of weeks of preparation and support from local makers, tradespeople and businesses.

Orla Bridal is now welcoming appointment bookings at The Chapel, Scout Road, Mytholmroyd.

Visit www.orlabridal.com or follow @orla.bridal on Instagram.

articles.title: East Lancashire Railway to host first Event, Catering and Retail Volunteer Open Day
articles.excerpt: East Lancashire Railway is inviting prospective volunteers to its first Event, Catering and Retail Volunteer Open Day at Bury Bolton Street Station on Monday 12 October.
articles.content_html:
East Lancashire Railway (ELR) is inviting prospective volunteers to its first Event, Catering and Retail Volunteer Open Day on Monday 12 October 2026.

The railway is looking for volunteers to help support a wide range of experiences, from luxury dining services and Rail Ale Trails to Days Out with Thomas and Santa Specials.

Volunteering opportunities cover events, catering and retail, with roles designed to suit a range of interests and experience. Volunteers could find themselves serving cream tea aboard a first-class carriage or helping to create the atmosphere for the Halloween Ghost Train.

The ELR said it will help match volunteers with roles that suit their interests and experience, with full training provided. No previous experience is needed.

Commercial Manager Lorna Kelly said: “If you’ve ever thought about volunteering at the East Lancashire Railway but felt unsure, or wondered whether you have the right experience, please come along to our Open Day. I’ll be there with some of our lovely volunteers, who can tell you what it’s really like to be part of the ELR.

“You can meet our events, catering and retail teams, hear about the roles available and ask any questions you have. Whether you’re ready to sign up or just curious, we’d love to meet you.”

The Open Day will take place at the Trackside Bar at Bury Bolton Street Station from 10am to 3pm on Monday 12 October.

The railway says prospective volunteers can attend to find out more about the roles available, meet members of the teams and ask questions before deciding whether to get involved.

Source: East Lancashire Railway.

articles.title: Rochdale’s Breaking Barriers secures core funding to expand its cultural work across Greater Manchester
articles.excerpt: Rochdale-based production company Breaking Barriers has secured three years of GMCA core funding to expand cultural programmes, paid opportunities and creative development across Greater Manchester.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale-based multidisciplinary production company Breaking Barriers has secured three years of core funding from the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) to strengthen the organisation and expand its cultural programmes across the region.

Over the funding period, Breaking Barriers plans to offer 42 paid placements through its Young Company programme, giving creatives aged 18–25 hands-on experience working on professional arts productions.

It will also provide 328 paid freelance roles and 45 in-kind artist residencies at its Rochdale base at Richard Street Studios.

Young Company participants will gain practical skills in producing, sound design, filmmaking and direction, with a focus on young people from underrepresented backgrounds who have had fewer opportunities to get into the arts.

A producer development programme will also support 36 creative producers a year to develop their own projects, secure resources and build sustainable careers.

Awarded through the Spirit strand of the GMCA Culture Fund, the investment will support Breaking Barriers to continue delivering theatre, film and immersive outdoor artworks, alongside training, mentoring and paid opportunities for emerging creatives.

Parvez Qadir, Artistic Director of Breaking Barriers, said: “Three years of core funding gives us the stability to plan ahead and grow as a company here in Rochdale. There’s so much creative talent locally, and we can now give more young people paid opportunities to work alongside experienced artists on our productions. It also enables us to keep building partnerships across Greater Manchester and develop projects shaped by local people, bringing their stories to life.”

Bev Craig, Mayor of Greater Manchester, said: “Culture has the power to connect communities, inspire creativity and strengthen pride in the places we call home.

“Through the Greater Manchester Culture Fund, we're investing in a diverse range of cultural organisations that help make our city region such a vibrant and inclusive place to live. Breaking Barriers is a fantastic example of a local company creating opportunities for young people to share their stories, develop their creativity and shape cultural experiences on their doorstep.”

Projects are currently planned to span the boroughs of Rochdale, Bury, Salford, Stockport, Manchester, Tameside and Bolton over three years.

Residents and local communities will help create outdoor artworks using sound, projection and light, alongside films and digital storytelling projects reflecting local experiences.

The funding will also help sustain and expand Breaking Barriers’ theatre in education work.

This includes multi-partnership delivery of Crossing the Line, a theatre and workshop programme tackling child criminal exploitation, which has already reached more than 15,000 young people across more than 220 schools.

Blind Side, exploring violence against women and girls, consent and healthy relationships, will continue to tour. Support from the Spirit strand will enable more time and resources to further expand its reach into other boroughs.

Source: Breaking Barriers.

articles.title: Sculpt & Edit launches wellness clinic after founder builds business from scratch
articles.excerpt: Sculpt & Edit founder Amy has opened a new wellness clinic after turning redundancy into an opportunity to build her own treatment business, with a focus on lymphatic drainage, post-surgery support and body treatments.
articles.content_html:
A new wellness clinic, Sculpt & Edit, has opened with a focus on treatments designed around body confidence, recovery and wellbeing.

Founder Amy said the clinic is intended to offer an alternative to a traditional beauty salon, bringing together lymphatic drainage and post-surgery support with body contouring and sculpting treatments.

The clinic will also offer more holistic treatments including Reiki and reflexology, alongside a growing focus on skin health and hydration. Amy said vitamin injections and IV wellness treatments will also form part of the clinic's offering.

The launch follows a significant career change for Amy, who said she lost her job at the beginning of 2026 and decided to take the risk of building a business of her own.

Over the following eight months, she has developed Sculpt & Edit from the ground up, initially through her treatment business before moving into a physical wellness clinic.

Alongside the business, Amy said she has built a TikTok following of nearly 100,000 people by sharing her experience of becoming self-employed, building a business and life as a mum.

She described the opening of the clinic as a major milestone after what she said had been a life-changing year, and hopes her experience will encourage other people considering starting their own business.

Sculpt & Edit is now welcoming clients at the new clinic, with further information about treatments and the business available directly from the clinic.

Source: Sculpt & Edit.
